cards.front: What a payments interview is really about
cards.back: Correctness, not scale: never charge twice, never lose a charge, and prove it afterwards while relying on a slow, sometimes silent processor.
About 115 a second, about 1,200 in a 10× sale. One well-tuned Postgres primary can handle it.

cards.front: Why amounts are integers in minor units
cards.back: Floats can't represent 0.10 exactly and some currencies have zero or three decimals. 4999 with EUR means €49.99.
Not failure: the charge may have succeeded with only the response lost. Mark the payment UNKNOWN and resolve it, never guess.
Stored with a unique constraint in the same transaction that creates the PENDING payment row. A repeat returns the stored result; a repeat in flight gets 409.

cards.front: Why not hold a transaction open across the processor call?
cards.back: A 3-second call holds row locks and connections; at 1,200 a second the pool runs out. Write intent, commit, call, then record the outcome in a new transaction.
UPDATE ... SET status='CAPTURED' WHERE id=$1 AND status='AUTHORIZED'. Zero rows changed means someone else moved it first; never overwrite.
For every transaction and currency, debits equal credits. Entries are append-only and mistakes are fixed with reversing entries.
Local steps with compensations: reserve stock (release), authorise card (void), confirm order. No shared database transaction across services.
The event is written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change, then relayed to Kafka, so events are never lost or invented.
Our ledger against the processor's daily settlement file and bank statements, joined on processor transaction ID, flagging every mismatch.

cards.front: How we stay out of most PCI scope
cards.back: The processor's hosted fields collect the card and return a token; our servers never see card numbers.

quiz.q: A processor call times out after 10 seconds. What should the payment service do?
choices: Mark it failed and let the buyer retry
Mark it UNKNOWN, then retry with the same idempotency key, query the processor or wait for the webhook
Retry immediately with a new key
Charge again and refund later if needed
quiz.why: A timeout may hide a successful charge, so it must be resolved, not guessed.

quiz.q: During a sale the database connection pool runs out even though throughput is only 1,200 a second. What is the likely bug?
choices: Transactions are held open across the processor call
The ledger is append-only
Idempotency keys have a unique constraint
Amounts are stored as integers
quiz.why: Each 1-3 s call holds a connection and locks; commit intent first, call, then update.

quiz.q: Reconciliation finds a charge in the processor's settlement file with no matching order. What most likely caused it?
choices: A refund exceeded the captured amount
A duplicate webhook
A payment left in UNKNOWN that was never resolved
Currency rounding
quiz.why: Processor-only items are usually unresolved unknowns; record intent first and resolve quickly.

quiz.q: A late 'authorised' webhook arrives for a payment that is already captured. What should the handler do?
choices: Set the status back to AUTHORIZED
Reverse the capture
Raise a ledger imbalance alert
Ignore it, since the guarded transition no longer applies
quiz.why: Handlers check current state and skip transitions already done or no longer valid.

quiz.q: The order service occasionally confirms an order whose payment was rolled back. What fixes this?
choices: A transactional outbox written in the same transaction as the state change
Publishing to Kafka before committing
Longer webhook retries
A second processor
quiz.why: The outbox guarantees events match committed state.

quiz.q: An engineer wants to fix a wrong seller balance by editing the ledger row. What is the right approach?
choices: Update the row and log it
Delete the row and insert a correct one
Append reversing and correcting entries
Edit the running balance table only
quiz.why: The ledger is append-only so history stays a complete audit trail.

quiz.q: Your only processor has an outage in the middle of a sale. What design choice keeps checkout working?
choices: Active-active payment databases
A second processor behind the PSP adapter, routed by health
Longer timeouts
Float amounts for speed
quiz.why: Two processors are a feature: the adapter fails over by health.
